title: Words, song and images (CCC 1153–1162)
hookLine: the one who sings prays twice, as the saying goes

lines: THE ONE WHO SINGS PRAYS TWICE.
cards: The one who sings prays twice. That's an old saying as the Catechism gives it, and it credits the line to Saint Augustine. A sentence spoken once is easy to lose by lunch.
A sentence sung tends to stay, sometimes for years, attached to a tune that comes back at a red light or in the shower. Yesterday, things: water, oil and bread.
Today, the other material of the liturgy: words spoken, words sung, and pictures on the walls.

teach.h: A CONVERSATION OF WORDS AND ACTIONS.
teach.b: First, words. The Catechism describes the liturgy as a meeting, a conversation between God and his people, carried by actions and words together.
That's why every sacrament comes with words: the water of baptism is poured while words are said.
The Word of God is read aloud, and the Catechism says the books, the place of reading, the way it's read and the listening all matter. Second, song.

teach.h: PSALMS, AND HYMNS, AND SPIRITUAL CANTICLES.
teach.b: Saint Paul tells the Ephesians to speak to one another "in psalms, and hymns, and spiritual canticles, singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord."
The Catechism sets that beside the saying about praying twice, and beside a story from Augustine's own life.
In the days of his baptism in Milan, he heard the church's hymns and wept. The voices flowed into his ears, he wrote, and the truth into his heart.
The Church's music, the Catechism says, should be beautiful, help people pray, and let the whole gathering join in, not just the choir. Third, images. The invisible God can't be pictured.

teach.h: GOD BECAME FLESH, AND COULD BE SEEN.
teach.b: But in Jesus, Catholics believe, God became flesh and could be seen. So an image of Christ isn't a guess at the invisible; it points to someone who was really seen.
Day seven hundred sixty heard John of Damascus make this case.
The Church honors images of Christ, Mary, the angels and the saints, and the honor, the Catechism says elsewhere, passes through the picture to the one pictured.
Fourth, they work together: ear, voice and eye, all saying one thing. Some people are moved by an argument. Augustine, by his own account, was moved to tears by a hymn.

how: At Mass Catholics hear scripture read aloud, sing psalms and hymns, and pray in churches decorated with images of Christ, Mary and the saints; Eastern Catholics venerate icons.

o: speech that carries the meeting of God and people
the printed hymn numbers posted on the wall
the fixed rules for how a priest must speak

games.q: you're Augustine, in the days of your baptism, standing in the church in Milan as the hymns begin. what happens?
o: you argue with the bishop about the words
you weep, as the truth flows into your heart
games.why: he wept. the voices flowed into his ears, he wrote, and the truth into his heart.

practice: Let one song come back to you: a hymn, a carol, a psalm, something sung at a wedding or a funeral or a school assembly long ago. Find one line and sing it softly, out loud if you can, under your breath if you can't.
If you pray, let the line be your prayer; if you don't, let it be a way of remembering the people you once sang it with.

wordCard.voice: Words. In the liturgy, words spoken and sung carry the meeting between God and his people, together with actions and images that point to Christ. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: sing it. A sung line tends to stay, sometimes for years. See you tomorrow.
